To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) uteroplacental hypoperfusion in mice on embryonic day 13.5 results in a transient increase in cerebral vascular density, which is associated with reduced neonatal excitotoxic brain lesions when the insult occurs at day 2 after birth; 2) this protection is lost when the neonatal insult occurs at day10.
uteroplacental hypoperfusion, a cause of intrauterine growth retardation, increases neonatal sensitivity to excitotoxicity.
uteroplacental hypoperfusion in mice is a useful model of fetal brain injury in humans.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of antenatal vascular intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR), a condition that occurs in about 10% of pregnancies, on neonatal microvascularisation and sensitivity to the excitotoxin ibotenate.
the role of the NMDA receptor (NMDAR) in the brain and its involvement in the pathogenesis of cerebral palsy (CP).

the study of the effect of antenatal vascular intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR), induced by unilateral uterine artery ligation (UAL) in the mouse, on neonatal microvasculature and on neonatal excitotoxic sensitivity to the NMDA agonist ibotenate
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neonatal brain is protected against neonatal excitotoxin sensitivity in the early phase of IUGR.

IUGR is associated with increased microvascular density, but that this may be insufficient to protect against neonatal excitotoxin-induced lesions, which are increased in the cortex and white matter after ibotenate administration on PD10.

the neonatal brain of mice subjected to antenatal IUGR, induced by a uterine laceration on day 13.5 of gestation, was more susceptible to NMDA receptor-mediated excitotoxicity than that of sham-operated animals when exposed to an intracerebral injection of the NMDA receptor agonist ibotenate on postnatal day 10, but less susceptible when injected on postnatal day two.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the IUGR mice are protected against neonatal NMDA excitotoxicity, but only when the insult is given at an earlier time point.
uteroplacental hypoperfusion during fetal development leads to increased angiogenic responses and decreased sensitivity to neonatal NMDA excitotoxicity in the cortex, but not in the WM.

uterine laceration in mice on E13.5, which causes a reduction in placental perfusion, leads to a reduction in fetal weight at birth, and that this is associated with a transient increase in angiogenesis in brain microvasculature.
The main takeaway from our work is that
vascular IUGR offers only transient protection against excitotoxic lesions in the brain of newborn mice, possibly via angiogenic mechanisms.
vascular IUGR is a model of transient neonatal protection from NMDA excitotoxicity.
